title: Study Abroad Report: Lund University
paragraphs: I was allowed to study at Lund University in Sweden for two months. Lund University is the second oldest university in Sweden, and its main campus is in Lund, in Skane County at the southernmost tip of Sweden. Lund is characterised by a refined Nordic townscape and good safety, and dormitory life there was very enjoyable, but my clerkship site was Malmo Hospital in the neighbouring city. Malmo has a high proportion of immigrants within Sweden, and as for safety, as its reputation suggested, I also felt it was worse than the Nordic image, but that too was a valuable experience.

At Malmo Hospital, I was looked after in neurology for the first month. A conference was held every day from 8 a.m., and it was impressive that people took part actively in the discussion regardless of their year. After that, I chose and joined the clerkship at the place that interested me among three: the outpatient clinic, consults from other departments, and standby on the semi-emergency ward. In the outpatient clinic, one hour was allotted per patient, and perhaps because there was very ample time, it was impressive that they spent more than 40 minutes on the interview. However, this interview was basically conducted in Swedish. Although they speak very fluent English, it is only natural that patients who have come to the hospital after waiting for months would try to convey their condition more accurately in their mother tongue, Swedish, but when they said that English was fine, I was able to spend the following hour very meaningfully, and I felt very grateful. Also, for the neurological examination, I could convey instructions to some extent through gestures even to patients who could not speak English, so I had a sense of having taken part in the examination at least a little. The number of consults from other departments and standby on the semi-emergency ward varied greatly from day to day, and in some cases there was only one in a morning. In that case, I asked the supervising doctors many questions. The lunch break was an hour and a half and the clerkship ended by 16:00 at the latest, so I could use the free time to prepare for the next day and study on my own, and it became a well-balanced clerkship.

For the next month I trained in the Vascular Unit. The Vascular Unit was a department combining surgery and internal medicine related to blood vessels. The start and end times were almost the same as in neurology, but the major difference in the content of the clerkship was that while neurology was mainly examination, the Vascular Unit was mainly treatment. I was told to choose whichever I liked from the operations and medical procedures that started around 9 every day, so I tried to experience as many kinds of cases as possible. Many doctors observed during treatment, so I actively asked questions.

What I strongly felt through this clerkship was that all the doctors speak English fluently and are enthusiastic about education, and that the working environment for doctors is greatly different from Japan's. It seems that the major reasons why Swedish doctors speak medical English fluently are that a certain number of doctors study at universities in other countries that are easier to enter, and that English medical books are used even domestically. In such an environment, I, whose mother tongue is not English, was also required to have the same level of medical English, and I remember feeling very much pressure. Also, as for the doctors' working environment, in both neurology and the Vascular Unit nobody worked more than 8 hours a day, and long vacations of more than a month, which I felt was very good. However, it was impressive that, as the doctors lamented that in that situation it is difficult to carry out screening tests as in Japan, balancing it with the quality of care is still hard.

I had long held a vague admiration for Nagoya University's study abroad program, and this study abroad was more fulfilling than I had imagined. The clerkship format was mostly observation, but I feel that I gained a great deal from the kindness and educational enthusiasm of the doctors at Lund University. I think that having been allowed such a valuable experience will be a treasure for life. I am grateful to the doctors of the International Collaboration Office, the doctors of the Frontier Association, and the many others who gave great support. Thank you.
